idiom_name: iterator helper chain over a real iterator (arr.values(), Map/Set iterator, generator)
implementation_notes: ES2025 iterator helpers give the language its native lazy composition: map, filter, take, drop, flatMap are methods on Iterator instances and return iterator helpers that only produce the next value when requested, so a chain consumes the source once and materializes only at toArray/reduce/forEach - and it can run over an infinite iterator. Start the chain from a real iterator (arr.values(), a generator, a Map/Set iterator), because Array.prototype.map/filter create a new array per stage. MDN marks the helpers Baseline 2025: use the generator variant where older runtimes must be supported.
code_sketch:
const total = people.values()
  .filter(p => p.age > 18)
  .map(p => p.score)
  .take(100)
  .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);   // one pass, no intermediate arrays
pitfalls: Iterator helpers need a real iterator: each Array.prototype.map/filter call in the chain materializes an array, so mixing the two styles keeps the allocations you meant to remove.
An iterator helper is single-use, like the iterator it wraps; keep the producing function (not the iterator) when the pipeline must run again.
Errors surface at the terminal call (reduce/toArray) far from the stage that threw; name the stages to keep traces readable.

variants.name: Generator-function pipeline (ES2015)
variants.implementation_notes: Before iterator helpers, generators were the portable lazy composition: each stage is a function* that pulls from its input with for..of and yields transformed elements, so the chain is a single pull path with one suspended frame per stage and no arrays. It runs wherever ES2015 does; the price is one generator frame per element per stage, which is why a plain loop still wins for short chains.
pitfalls: Generators are single-use and their bodies run only when pulled, so error timing moves to the consumer.
Deep generator chains add a suspended frame per element per stage, which shows up in profiles as generator overhead.

variants.name: Transducer composition (library)
variants.idiom_name: compose(map(f), filter(p)) applied by reduce/transduce (Ramda-style transducer libraries)
variants.implementation_notes: The library route makes the transformation itself a value: a transducer is a function from reducer to reducer, so map/filter/take compose with ordinary function composition and are applied once per element by the consumer's reduce loop - they compose directly, without awareness of the input or creation of intermediate aggregates. JavaScript libraries (Ramda's transducers, transducers-js) provide this on top of reduce/transduce. Choose it when one transformation vocabulary must be reused across sources and sinks, not for a single pipeline.
variants.code_sketch:
const xform = R.compose(R.filter(p => p.age > 18), R.map(p => p.score));
const total = R.reduce(R.add, 0, R.transduce(xform, R.add, 0, people));
pitfalls: Transducers are reduce-shaped: stages that need the whole collection (sort, reverse, group) cannot be transducers and force a boundary.
The library adds an abstraction and a dependency for what a short chain states directly in the language.
